title: Paying Foreign Contractors: W-8BEN, 1099 Rules, and Where an EOR Is Required
summary: 1099 for foreign contractors: why Form W-8BEN replaces it, when IRS 30% withholding and Form 1042-S apply, and the R&D credit catch. Learn what to file.
body_markdown:
## What Paying a Foreign Contractor Triggers


A 1099 for foreign contractors is usually not required, but the paperwork that replaces it has to be on file before the first payment goes out.


Paying international contractors is documentation-first, not year-end-first. The W-8 instructions tell the payee to deliver the certificate before income is paid or credited. A company that wires money in March and starts chasing forms the following January has already created the exposure, and a form signed later doesn’t cure the payments that already left.


The first payment forces three questions, and each one points at a different form and a different penalty.


- **Is the payee a US person?** US citizens and green-card holders are US persons no matter where they live, so they get a Form W-9 and a Form 1099-NEC. Everyone else certifies foreign status on Form W-8BEN as an individual or Form W-8BEN-E as an entity.
- **Where were the services physically performed?** Services are sourced where the work happens. Work performed abroad is foreign-source income under IRC 862(a)(3) and sits outside Chapter 3 withholding. Work performed on US soil is US-source under IRC 861(a)(3), and the whole withholding machine switches on.
- **Is this a contractor relationship under the law of the country where the person sits?** No US form answers this. A W-8BEN certifies tax residency, not employment status.


The forms follow the work, not the contract.


What the first payment does not create is worth naming too. A foreign contractor working entirely abroad creates no US state payroll registration, no Form 941 obligation, no FICA liability, and no W-2. The engineering spend does immediately change your R&D credit base and your Section 174 position. Those two consequences fire silently on the first invoice and show up a year later on the return.


Here’s the part most guides skip. Foreign-source compensation isn’t an amount subject to withholding, so there’s no Chapter 3 tax to withhold and no Form 1042-S to file. But an empty file isn’t neutral. The IRS[presumption rules](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/presumption-rules) state that if you cannot reliably associate a payment with valid documentation, you must apply the presumption rules or you may be liable for tax, interest, and penalties. Under Treas. Reg. 1.1441-1(b)(3) and 1.6049-5(d), an undocumented payee can be presumed a US person. That presumption converts a non-reportable payment into a reportable one.


The W-8BEN is never filed with the IRS. You keep it as the evidence that the presumption never had to be applied, which is why indinero treats the W-8 file as a controlled record rather than a folder, maintained alongside the[business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) work it protects.


## Federal Requirements


Federal compliance on a 1099 for foreign contractors has four moving parts. The W-8 certificate, collected before payment and refreshed on a three-year cycle. The source-of-income determination under IRC 861 and 862. The withholding and 1042-S reporting that switch on the moment work happens in the US. And the US-person override that puts American citizens abroad back on a 1099-NEC.


### Form 1099-NEC, the US person test, and the new $2,000 threshold


Form 1099-NEC is an information return for payments to US persons. The[IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) route foreign payees elsewhere in one line, directing filers to use Form 1042-S for payments to nonresident aliens.


The threshold moved, and nearly every competing guide is still printing the old one. OBBBA section 70433(a) raised the IRC 6041 base threshold to $2,000 for payments made after December 31, 2025, with new IRC 6041(h) indexing it for inflation for calendar years after 2026. Treasury and the IRS estimated that roughly 19.54 million of a projected 62.72 million Forms 1099-NEC would fall out of the filing population because of the change. The January 31 filing deadline is unchanged.


The US-person override is absolute. A US citizen or lawful permanent resident writing code from Lisbon is still a US person and still gets a Form 1099-NEC once payments reach $2,000. Residence abroad changes that contractor’s own return. It does not change your information-reporting duty. If you’re sorting out which payee gets which form, start with[the 1099 form types and what each one reports](https://www.indinero.com/blog/types-of-1099-forms/) .


### W-8BEN for contractors, and the three-year clock


W-8BEN for a foreign individual. W-8BEN-E for a foreign entity. Both are given to you, retained by you, and never filed with the IRS. Both are due before the first payment.


The validity window is the part companies underestimate. A Form W-8BEN remains in effect from the date it’s signed through the last day of the third succeeding calendar year, unless a change in circumstances makes the information incorrect. A form signed in any month of 2026 expires December 31, 2029. Every contractor onboarded in the same year expires on the same date, so the renewal workload arrives as one December spike unless someone is tracking signature dates as a data field.


Three details from the[instructions for Form W-8BEN](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/iw8ben) decide whether a certificate in your file is actually valid:


- **The 30-day change-in-circumstances rule.** The payee must notify you within 30 days and file a new form. The instructions flag that a change to a US address is itself a change in circumstances for foreign-status purposes.
- **The electronic signature standard.** Simply typing a name into the signature line is not an electronic signature. The form needs a time and date stamp plus a statement that it was electronically signed by a person authorized to do so. Most lightweight intake workflows fail this.
- **Line 6a, the foreign TIN.** Required from the jurisdiction of tax residence unless the payee is in a US territory or the jurisdiction appears on the IRS list of jurisdictions that don’t issue foreign TINs.


For entities, line 5 of the W-8BEN-E carries the Chapter 4 FATCA status, and most statuses require completing a supplementary certification part of the form. A two-person development shop in Poland is typically an Active NFFE and has to complete that part. An incomplete Chapter 4 status is the most common reason a W-8BEN-E on file isn’t a valid certificate.


### Source of income, and what changes on US soil


IRC 861(a)(3) sources compensation for services performed in the United States to the US. IRC 862(a)(3) sources compensation for services performed outside it to foreign sources. The IRS puts the rule plainly on its[source of income guidance](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/source-of-income-personal-service-income) : the location where services are performed controls, regardless of contract location, payment location, or payer residence.


There’s a de minimis exception in IRC 861(a)(3), and it almost never helps. It requires a nonresident alien temporarily present in the US for no more than 90 days in the tax year, compensation of no more than $3,000 in the aggregate, and a contract with a foreign person not engaged in a US trade or business. A week of onsite engineering at normal rates blows through the $3,000 ceiling.


When work is split, the IRS uses a time fraction: total compensation multiplied by US workdays divided by total workdays. Which is why the onsite trip has to be logged in days, not remembered in March.


Run it on a real pattern. You pay a Buenos Aires contractor $9,000 a month and fly him to Austin for a 10-day sprint in June. Ten US workdays out of 240 makes roughly $4,500 of $108,000 US-source. The de minimis exception is unavailable. Absent a valid treaty claim, IRC 1441(a) requires 30 percent, so $1,350 of Chapter 3 tax. That sits above $200 and below $2,000, so under the[instructions for Form 1042](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1042) it has to be deposited within 15 days after the end of the month it was withheld, through EFTPS or IRS Direct Pay. The payment then goes on a Form 1042-S due March 15, with a Form 1042 filed alongside. Reporting is required even when a treaty eliminates the tax entirely. Zero dollars of this appears on a 1099-NEC.


### Backup withholding, Form 8233, and the penalty math


The 24 percent figure quoted all over this topic is real, but the mechanism is usually described wrong. Backup withholding doesn’t attach because a contractor is foreign. It attaches because an empty file lets the presumption rules treat an undocumented payee as a US person, which converts a non-reportable foreign-source payment into a reportable 1099 payment subject to backup withholding. You then owe tax you never withheld, plus penalties on returns you never filed.


Form 8233 is the route when a nonresident alien claims treaty-based exemption from withholding on personal services, including contract labor and consulting fees. Three mechanics trip up first-time filers. A US TIN is mandatory, so a contractor without an SSN needs an ITIN first, which lengthens onboarding materially. You have to forward a copy to the IRS within 5 days of accepting it. And you must wait at least 10 days after mailing it to see whether the IRS objects, so paying exempt on day one is a procedural failure even when the treaty claim is good.


The penalty schedule is per return, and it applies separately to the failure to file with the IRS and the failure to furnish the payee statement. For 2026 the IRS figures run $60 up to 30 days late, $130 from 31 days late through August 1, $340 after August 1 or not filed, and $680 for intentional disregard, which carries no maximum. That’s how a 25-contractor documentation failure becomes a five-figure assessment before any tax is counted.


## State Requirements


A foreign contractor performing services entirely outside the United States creates no state payroll registration, no state income tax withholding, and no state unemployment insurance account. State obligations attach to where work is physically performed, which makes the offshore engagement the one hiring pattern that is genuinely clean at the state layer. Three things break that.


**The contractor relocates into a US state.** The moment services are performed from a US location, that state’s rules engage, and the thresholds are low enough to be useless as a buffer. The[California EDD](https://edd.ca.gov/en/payroll_Taxes/Am_I_Required_to_Register_as_an_Employer) requires an employer to register within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages in a calendar quarter, and registration brings Unemployment Insurance, Employment Training Tax, State Disability Insurance, and Personal Income Tax withholding with it. One relocating engineer clears $100 in a single pay period. This is also why the W-8BEN 30-day change-in-circumstances rule is a state control and not only a federal one. A contractor who moves to San Diego and doesn’t refile is carrying an invalid federal certificate and an unregistered state employer at the same time. Our guide to[multi-state payroll compliance for growing SaaS](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-state-payroll-compliance-for-growing-saas/) covers the registration sequence that follows.


**A US-resident contractor who is really an employee.** That’s a domestic classification question decided by the state’s own test, and getting it wrong produces back withholding, back FICA, and back unemployment contributions. We cover where those lines actually fall in[employee versus contractor status](https://www.indinero.com/blog/employee-vs-contractor/) .


**An employer of record or local-entity hire.** The employer of record vs contractor decision creates foreign payroll registration, not US state registration. Hiring through an EOR or standing up a local subsidiary produces local payroll accounts, withholding at source, social contributions, statutory leave, and local termination rules. None of it appears on a Form 941. It appears as a monthly invoice with an employer-burden line that belongs next to the contractor rate in your model. Social security double taxation is the piece companies forget. The US maintains totalization agreements with several nations to avoid double taxation on social security taxes, and claiming the exemption requires a Certificate of Coverage from the home country’s social security agency. No certificate, no exemption, and the contribution gets paid twice.


Say the quiet part. Offshore contracting really is cheaper at the US state layer. The cost didn’t disappear. It moved to the contractor’s country and to your R&D credit.


## Common Mistakes


Five of the six failures below cost money. One of them can cost multiples of the entire contract value, and no US form prevents it.


1.


**Paying first and collecting the W-8 later.** The most common failure and the easiest to fix. Both W-8 instruction sets require the certificate before payment is made or credited. Payments already out the door sit in the presumption regime, with backup withholding and unfiled 1099s as the downside. The fix is a payment-rail control, not a policy document. No vendor record is payable until a signed, complete, unexpired W-8 is attached.


2.


**Treating a foreign worker as a contractor when local law calls them an employee.** This is the expensive one, and US tax forms are irrelevant to it. Foreign contractor classification is decided by the labor authority where the person sits, and in most jurisdictions it turns on control, exclusivity, integration into the business, and economic dependence, assessed on facts rather than contract labels.[Directive (EU) 2024/2831](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831/oj) on platform work directs that status be guided primarily by the facts relating to the actual performance of work, and applies its presumption of employment to ongoing relationships for periods starting from 2 December 2026. The Dutch Tax Administration has enforced against false self-employment under the Wet DBA since 1 January 2025, where the client is treated as the employer and faces an additional payroll tax assessment. The UK’s off-payroll rules decide who carries the tax and National Insurance, with HMRC’s Check Employment Status for Tax tool giving its view on the facts you provide. Philippine courts apply a four-fold test in which control over means and methods is decisive, and the employer carries the burden of proving contractor status. The pattern is the same everywhere. Full-time hours you set, exclusivity, your equipment, your management chain, and years of tenure flip the classification. Which describes most offshore engineering arrangements exactly.


3.


**Missing the 1042-S when any work happened in the US.** The onsite sprint, the offsite, the conference booth, the onboarding week in your office. All of it creates US-source compensation and a Form 1042-S obligation, and the 1042-S is due even when a treaty wipes out the tax. Companies that correctly conclude “no 1099” frequently conclude “no reporting at all,” which is only true when US workdays are zero.


4.


**Letting W-8BENs expire.** The three-succeeding-calendar-year clock kills every certificate signed in a given year on the same December 31. Few companies store the signature date as a tracked field, and an expired W-8 is functionally identical to no W-8 for presumption purposes.


5.


**Assuming an EOR removes classification risk.** An EOR genuinely resolves local employment classification for the workers it employs, because they’re employees of its local entity. It doesn’t cover workers you keep engaging directly alongside the EOR population, it doesn’t remove permanent establishment risk created by what those people actually do, and it doesn’t change the R&D credit treatment of the spend by a dollar.


6.


**Creating permanent establishment exposure through a long-term exclusive contractor.** The[US Model Income Tax Convention](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/131/Treaty-US-Model-2016_1.pdf) defines a permanent establishment as a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on, and treats a dependent agent as creating one where a person habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts binding on the enterprise. A country sales lead abroad with signing authority is the textbook exposure. A back-end engineer with no customer-facing authority usually isn’t. Treaty definitions vary, so the governing treaty decides.


## The R&D Credit + Payroll Connection


Research has to be conducted in the United States to qualify.[IRC 41(d)(4)(F)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/41) excludes any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States from qualified research, and the Form 6765 instructions repeat it under excluded activities. Offshoring an engineering team therefore shrinks the credit base and the payroll offset at the same time. Since the 2025 legislation it also pushes the underlying spend onto a 15-year amortization schedule.


This is the section no payment rail and no global-employment platform writes, and it’s the number that decides whether the offshore rate card actually wins.


### The three-line hierarchy


For R&D credit purposes, a dollar of qualified US employee wage is worth a dollar of qualified research expense, because IRC 41(b)(2)(B) treats employee compensation for qualified services as fully includible in-house research. A dollar paid to a US contractor for qualified research is worth 65 cents, because IRC 41(b)(3)(A) counts only 65 percent of amounts paid to a non-employee, rising to 75 percent for a qualified research consortium. A dollar paid to a contractor performing the work abroad is worth zero.


That’s the whole decision in three lines, and it’s the comparison that belongs in the hiring model rather than in a post-mortem on the return.


### The payroll offset shrinks with the credit


For a pre-profit company, the research credit becomes real cash only through the payroll tax election. The election is made in Section D of Form 6765, line 33a, no later than the due date of the originally filed return including extensions. A qualified small business needs gross receipts under $5 million for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the tax year. The elected amount then flows to[Form 8974](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i8974) and lands on Forms 941, 943, or 944, capped at $500,000 per year since the Inflation Reduction Act raised it from $250,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022. The first $250,000 applies against the employer share of social security tax per quarter, then against Medicare, with the remainder carried forward.


Now stack the two effects. Move engineering offshore and the qualified research base falls, the credit falls, and the Form 8974 offset against quarterly Form 941 liability falls with it. You reduce payroll tax liability and simultaneously reduce the credit available to offset what’s left. Part of the offshore saving is funded by giving up a dollar-for-dollar federal offset worth up to $500,000 a year. The quarter-by-quarter mechanics of[applying the R&D credit against payroll taxes](https://www.indinero.com/blog/rd-tax-credit-against-payroll-taxes/) show where that cash actually lands.


### Section 174A, and the same statutory test twice


OBBBA section 70302(a) added IRC 174A, which allows a current deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures, effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. The same legislation amended IRC 174 so that it now applies only to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which continue to be amortized ratably over 15 years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year.


Here’s the cross-reference that makes this one rule instead of two.[Rev. Proc. 2025-28](https://www.irs.gov/irb/2025-38_IRB) section 2.04(3) defines domestic research or experimental expenditures by excluding amounts attributable to foreign research within the meaning of section 41(d)(4)(F). The exact test that disqualifies offshore engineering from the research credit also disqualifies it from current-year expensing.


One geographic line, two tax consequences.


The asymmetry is large enough to change a build decision. A million dollars of domestic engineering R&E is deductible in full in the year incurred and feeds the credit base. The same million spent on work performed abroad is amortized over 15 years from the midpoint of the year, delivering roughly $33,000 of deduction in year one and no research credit at all. Two deadlines are worth putting on the calendar now. The small business retroactive election under Rev. Proc. 2025-28 reaches back to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 for taxpayers inside the IRC 448(c) gross receipts test, stated as $31,000,000 for 2025, and it has to be made by July 6, 2026. The same date governs the related IRC 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit elections, which is why the credit study and the 174A position have to be modeled by one team rather than two advisors. Our breakdown of[Section 174 capitalization under current law](https://www.indinero.com/blog/section-174-rd-capitalization-explained-2026/) walks the transition rules in detail.


Indinero models this before the hire, not after the return.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up on nearly every engagement, usually in the week the first international offer gets signed or the week a state notice arrives. Here are the answers we give most often.


### Do you issue a 1099 to a contractor who lives outside the US?


A contractor living outside the US generally gets no Form 1099-NEC, because compensation for services performed abroad is foreign-source income under IRC 862(a)(3). They certify foreign status on Form W-8BEN instead, which you keep on file rather than send to the IRS. The one exception is the US-person override. A US citizen or green-card holder abroad still gets a 1099-NEC once payments reach $2,000. Indinero sorts which payee lands on which form before the first payment, not in January.


### What is Form W-8BEN and when do you have to collect it?


Form W-8BEN is the IRS certificate a foreign individual uses to document foreign status, and it’s due before the first payment. Foreign entities use Form W-8BEN-E. Neither goes to the IRS. You keep it as proof the presumption rules never had to apply. A W-8BEN stays valid through the third succeeding calendar year, so one signed in 2026 expires December 31, 2029. Indinero tracks signature dates as a field, so renewals don’t arrive as one December surprise.


### When does a payment to a foreign contractor require withholding and Form 1042-S?


Withholding and Form 1042-S attach when the contractor performs services on US soil, which makes that portion of the pay US-source income. IRC 1441(a) then requires 30 percent withholding unless a valid treaty claim reduces it. The 1042-S is due March 15 even when a treaty wipes the tax to zero, with Form 1042 filed alongside it. A single onsite sprint triggers all of it, which is why indinero captures US workdays per contractor during the year.


### When should you use an employer of record instead of a contractor agreement?


Use an employer of record when the working relationship would make the person an employee under the law of the country where they sit. Full-time hours you set, exclusivity, your equipment, and long tenure flip the classification. An employer of record resolves that question for the workers it employs. It doesn’t change the R&D credit treatment of the spend or remove permanent establishment risk. Indinero prices the contractor, employer of record, and US employee options side by side before the hire.


### Can offshore engineering contractor spend count toward the R&D tax credit?


Offshore engineering spend generates no R&D tax credit, because IRC 41(d)(4)(F) excludes research conducted outside the United States from qualified research. A dollar of US employee wage is worth a dollar of qualified research expense. A dollar to a US contractor is worth 65 cents. A dollar offshore is worth zero. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 applies the same test to Section 174A, so foreign research stays on 15-year amortization instead of current expensing. Indinero models that gap before the hire.


### What is permanent establishment risk and how does a contractor create it?


Permanent establishment risk is the chance a country treats your business as having a taxable presence there and taxes the profits attributable to it. Under the US Model Income Tax Convention, a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts binding on your company can create one. A country sales lead abroad with signing authority is the textbook exposure. A back-end engineer usually isn’t. Treaty definitions vary, so the governing treaty decides, not the job title on the contract.


### Does a US citizen working abroad get a W-2 or a 1099?


A US citizen working abroad gets a W-2 as an employee and a 1099-NEC as a contractor, because citizenship keeps them a US person. Location doesn’t decide the form. The relationship does. Issuing a 1099-NEC to a citizen abroad who functions as an employee doesn’t convert them into a contractor. Social security coverage is a separate question, and claiming relief under a totalization agreement requires a Certificate of Coverage from the home country’s agency.
